title: Creating and Using Views
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Creating and Using Views.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to create view.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Creating and Using Views. Its primary job is to help you organize multi-stage SQL into views, CTEs and reusable reporting patterns that remain understandable. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing creating and using views teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: organize multi-stage SQL into views, CTEs and reusable reporting patterns that remain understandable. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Creating and Using Views
content_blocks.code:
CREATE VIEW available_products AS
SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE available = true;
content_blocks.expected_output: Creates a view definition over the selected products rows when the source table and columns exist.
content_blocks.safety_note: DDL should be applied in a scratch database; recursive queries need a clear termination condition.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Assumes a disposable schema with a products table unless the query is self-contained.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Creating and Using Views”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “CREATE VIEW”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “CREATE VIEW”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Creating and Using Views, with an explanation of “CREATE VIEW”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Creating and Using Views fits into the broader goal to organize multi-stage SQL into views, CTEs and reusable reporting patterns that remain understandable.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: CREATE VIEW, Naming and organizing views, Encapsulating complex queries.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
